source.title: Evaluating Risks in Weak-to-Strong Alignment: A Bias-Variance Perspective
source.authors: Hamid Osooli; Kareema Batool; Rick Gentry; Tiasa Singha Roy; Ashwin Gupta; Anirudha Ramesh

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including supplementary material; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates weak-to-strong pipelines using held-out blind-spot deception rather than Burns et al.'s PGR. The deception measure directly tests the V4 failure mode of confident strong-model errors where the weak model is uncertain, but it does not test whether the strong model beats the weak supervisor.
record.gate_note: The study does not report weak-to-strong performance versus weak-model performance or a strong-model ceiling, so it does not test PGR (V1). It compares pipeline variants, but does not measure PGR improvements from the changes (V2), PGR dependence on size/task/representation (V3), distribution shift or shared-error effects (V4 subparts). Table 3 reports blind-spot deception scores and counts at five thresholds; rows record the scores. Table 2 also reports broad deception at τ = 0.25; those results are included as related but broader than the blind-spot failure mode. BVC correlations are diagnostic associations with deception, not measurements of PGR.
record.test_reason: The study trains Llama-3.1-8B on labels from a Llama-3.2-3B weak model in four SFT/RLHF/RLAIF pipelines. It measures held-out blind-spot deception: confident strong-model errors where the weak model is uncertain. This operationalises the V4 failure mode of errors in regions the weak supervisor cannot check. It is a different method from Burns et al. aimed at the failure question. No baseline or control (e.g. a ground-truth-trained strong model) is reported, so the scores are levels only.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude strong-model variance is the BVC quantity most associated with blind-spot deception. They also conclude that weak-model training shapes where blind spots arise, and that the metric diagnoses failures without a ceiling model. They stress the findings are exploratory (n=8 settings) and that mitigation is not demonstrated.
record.recipe_differences: Uses four SFT/RLHF/RLAIF pipeline combinations and evaluates blind-spot deception and confidence-based BVC quantities; does not use Burns et al.'s PGR or compare student performance with supervisor and ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: Blind-spot deception changes with threshold τ, dataset, and weak-model training procedure; the leading pipeline differs across the two datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Broad deception (a confident strong error where the weak model is not confidently correct) is nonzero in all settings at τ=0.25. RLHF⇒RLAIF is highest on both datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Broad confident-error rates mix inherited weak-model errors with blind-spot errors.

fits_no_version.finding: Strong-model confidence variance correlates with blind-spot deception across 8 settings (Spearman ρ=0.929; 0.893 with the outlier removed).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Strong-model confidence dispersion predicts weak-to-strong blind-spot failures.

record.code_released: not stated (the reproducibility statement gives the code location as “--”)
record.problems: The authors describe the correlation findings as exploratory because they involve only eight pipeline–dataset settings. Experiments use only Llama-family models and safety/harmlessness preference data. Confidence is used as a proxy for reward-like quantities; the paper reports three runs but gives no per-row uncertainty intervals. Deception scores are threshold-sensitive. The paper does not demonstrate that its diagnostics mitigate failures.
record.rows_left_out: The 40 broad-deception threshold-sweep values in Supplementary Table 4 were not extracted because that measure is broader than the weak-uncertainty blind-spot behavior; Table 2 broad-deception results at τ = 0.25 are retained as related findings. BVC component values and correlation statistics were not included as rows because they are diagnostics/predictors rather than PGR or the specified blind-spot behavior. No results were omitted for the tested V4 blind-spot metric.

untested.parts: No weak accuracy, strong ceiling or PGR is reported.
No training change is evaluated for PGR gains.
There is one weak/strong size pair and no PGR sweep. BVC correlations predict deception, not PGR.
Distribution shift and shared-error shrinkage of gains are not tested. No control for blind-spot deception is reported (e.g. a strong model trained on ground truth).
A misfit risk bound is derived, but not conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.

missing.what: Strong-model error counts: 2339–2802 of 5000 held-out pairs, i.e. strong accuracy near chance. Weak accuracy is not reported, so V1 cannot be computed.

record.verdict_notes: The partial/absent/observed cut-offs are relative: there is no baseline, so states compare each score with the dominant pipeline at the same τ. Values ≤0.01 are treated as absent. The strong models err on roughly half of held-out pairs, so weak-to-strong success itself is doubtful but unmeasured. Code is not released (link given as '--').

versions.untested_parts: No weak-supervisor performance, strong-model ceiling, or PGR is reported.
Pipeline variants are compared on deception, not on whether a training change raises PGR over naive fine-tuning.
No PGR sweep across model sizes, tasks, or representations; only Llama-family models on two safety/harmlessness preference datasets are used.
Tests blind-spot deception where the strong model is confidently wrong and the weak model is uncertain. Does not test distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong errors are alike.
Derives a misfit-based risk bound, but does not test conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality is studied.

relationships.display_finding: The share of strong-model errors that are confident and occur where the weak model is uncertain is 0.36–0.53 on PKU and 0.13–0.26 on HH; no control baseline was used.

source_check.reason: Table 3 reports substantial blind-spot error fractions in these conditions, supporting the operational failure mode; strategic exploitation and excess over a control are not established.

relationships.reason: With an SFT strong stage, scores are low (≤0.12) and near zero at τ≥0.30 (r01–r05, r11–r15, r21–r25, r31–r35). Which weak-model pipeline dominates depends on the dataset, and scores depend on the choice of τ.
relationships.display_finding: Scores are at most 0.12 and approach zero at τ≥0.30; their magnitude depends on τ, and the highest-scoring weak-model pipeline varies by dataset.

labels.reason: The scores depend on pipeline, dataset and threshold and are substantially smaller with SFT strong stages. The exact maximum is 0.122; several near-zero scores retain nonzero counts.

relation.reason: Reports held-out rates of confident strong-model errors in weak-model uncertainty regions across training pipelines and thresholds.

tranche.reason: Tests weak-to-strong blind-spot failures using preference-training pipelines and a confidence-conditioned error metric rather than the original method and PGR measure.

source_check.notes: The text is arXiv v3, dated 4 August 2026. Results average three seeds; the authors describe eight-setting correlations as exploratory and explicitly distinguish their diagnostic from proof of strategic intent or demonstrated mitigation.

statements.correction: PKU RLHF⇒RLAIF: 0.477, 0.525, 0.362 at τ=0.10, 0.20, 0.30. HH SFT⇒RLAIF: 0.261, 0.219, 0.127. Weak/strong designations use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; no independent capability comparison reported. Three-seed averaging and correlation p-values reported; no per-score uncertainty intervals.
statements.problem: The scores and model identities match, but the asserted capability check is not reported as a direct weak-versus-strong capability comparison.

statements.correction: Maximum SFT-strong score: 0.122, PKU RLHF⇒SFT, τ=0.10. PKU SFT⇒SFT scores at τ=0.30 and 0.40 round to 0.000 but each has numerator 1 of 2494.
statements.problem: The exact SFT-strong maximum is 0.122, exceeding the stated bound of 0.12. The other quoted scores and counts match.

statements.correction: Four pipelines include SFT⇒SFT and RLHF⇒SFT. SFT⇒SFT trains the strong policy on weak-preferred responses without reward modeling. SFT-strong maximum: 0.122. Blind-spot deception measures confident errors during weak-model uncertainty; strategic intent is not established.
statements.problem: The SFT-strong bound excludes 0.122. The study includes plain SFT on weak-preferred responses, so describing all its evidence as requiring RL or an incentive is too broad; its diagnostic also does not establish strategic exploitation.

statements.correction: SFT-strong maximum: 0.122. PKU RLHF⇒RLAIF scores at τ=0.10, 0.20, 0.30: 0.477, 0.525, 0.362.
statements.problem: The pipeline comparison is supported, but the exact SFT-strong maximum is 0.122 rather than ≤0.12.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Evaluated pipelines on PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF at τ values with nonzero blind-spot scores
reader_labels.reason: Blind-spot deception is observed in these weak-to-strong settings, with scores varying across datasets, pipelines and thresholds (r01–r02, r06–r09, r11–r13, r16–r20, r21–r24, r26–r30, r31–r34, r36–r40). This supports occurrence of the specified failure mode, not PGR claims.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Threshold-sensitive scores and zero-score cases; relative pipeline ranking differs between datasets
reader_labels.reason: Scores generally decline as τ increases, some settings report 0.000, and the paper reports RLHF ⇒ RLAIF highest on PKU-SafeRLHF but SFT ⇒ RLAIF highest on HH-RLHF; the effect is conditional rather than uniform (r03–r05, r10, r14–r15, r25, r35, r01–r40).
